sections.h2: Who runs Lucas County property tax?
sections.html:
Two county offices share the work, both at One Government Center in Toledo. The Auditor sets values, keeps the tax records, accepts Board of Revision complaints and takes homestead applications. The Treasurer mails the bills, collects payments and handles delinquent parcels. Reach the Auditor at 419-213-4406. The Treasurer is in Suite 500.

Lucas County takes in 596 square miles of northwest Ohio along Lake Erie and the Maumee River. Toledo serves as the seat and has the most residents, with Sylvania, Maumee, Oregon and Waterville as the other cities and Holland, Ottawa Hills and Whitehouse among the villages, per Wikipedia. The city or village and school district of your parcel shape its bill.

sections.h2: How is a Lucas County property tax bill calculated?
sections.html:
The Auditor's All About Property Taxes guide describes two steps. First, the property's market value is converted to a 35 percent assessed value. Second, that assessed value is multiplied by the tax rate for the taxing district and divided by 1,000.

The guide stresses that voters, not appraisers, set the rate through levies. As printed in its 2023 example, the rate for Sylvania city and Sylvania City School District was 82.695213, while Toledo city and Toledo City School District was 66.241870. The guide adds that Ohio taxes real property one year in the rear, so a bill paid in 2026 is for tax year 2025.

It also explains two older state credits. A 10 percent non-business credit and a 2.5 percent owner-occupied credit exist, but neither applies to levies passed after 2014, including replacement levies, so they do not cut the whole bill by those percentages. Look at your bill to see what credits it shows.

sections.h2: What are the Lucas County payment deadlines?
sections.html:
Each bill has two installments, with the due dates printed on it. The Treasurer's site states that the next due date is posted once bills are mailed. Under section 323.17, a delayed tax duplicate can push the payment dates to January 31 and July 20, which is why the dates can shift from year to year.

The Treasurer's site carries an important warning about mailing a payment. USPS postmarks can show a date a day or more after you mail, and Ohio law uses the postmark to decide whether a payment is on time. The office suggests three fixes:

  • Mail the check well ahead of the due date.
  • Ask for a hand-stamped postmark at the post office counter.
  • Pay online, which the site says is available at any time.

The Treasurer also lists a payment plan option on its home page. Ask that office for the terms before you fall behind.

sections.h2: How do I contest a Lucas County value?
sections.html:
Complaints go to the Board of Revision from January 1 through the end of March. On its Board of Revision page, the Auditor lists three board seats: Auditor, Treasurer and one Commissioner, or their delegates. Value is the only subject it hears. Rate and levy complaints are outside its reach.

Lucas County Board of Revision steps as the Auditor describes them
StepWhat the page says
Filing windowJanuary 1 to March 31
FormDTE Form 1, 1M or 2, filed on paper (notarized) or online
Hearing30-minute slot, in person, by phone or by video
EvidenceSubmit at least 5 days before the hearing
AttendanceRecommended, not required
Further appealBoard of Tax Appeals or Court of Common Pleas, 30 days counted from the date the decision was mailed

The owner must prove the case. The Auditor's guide points to nearby comparable sales, your own recent purchase price or a private appraisal. For a house damaged or torn down, a separate DTE 26 application adjusts value starting the next tax year.

sections.h2: What happens to my tax while a complaint is pending?
sections.html:
You may pay based on your own figure. Section 5715.19 requires the Treasurer to accept a payment computed on the value stated in your complaint while the complaint is pending. If the final value turns out higher than what you paid, interest runs on the shortfall from the original due date, so keep the complaint number handy when you pay.

The statute sets other rules worth knowing before you file:

  • Filing is open until March 31 or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later.
  • The board has 180 days after the last filing day to rule.
  • A second complaint on a parcel in the same interim period needs a changed fact, such as a sale at arm's length, a casualty loss or a major improvement.
  • Hold nothing back: evidence you keep from the board may be barred on appeal.

sections.h2: Which Lucas County tax relief programs can a seller or heir use?
sections.html:
The Auditor's homestead exemption page describes four tracks. Owners aged 65 and up, plus owners who are totally and permanently disabled, can claim it for the home they live in if 2025 taxable income was $41,000 or less; Social Security does not count, but a spouse's taxable income does. Disabled veterans rated or compensated at 100 percent qualify without an income limit. Surviving spouses of first responders killed in the line of duty can qualify for an enhanced version.

For tax year 2025, payable in 2026, the page says the exempted value is $29,000, and that amount doubles for disabled veterans and the surviving spouses. The exemption comes off the taxable value of the primary residence only. Questions go to Homestead@co.lucas.oh.us or 419-213-4406.

When the home sells, Ohio's value statement asks the buyer to confirm with the seller whether the property carries these reductions or the agricultural use valuation, as section 319.202 requires. Be honest on that form, since a reduction may end with the sale.

sections.h2: What does the Lucas County housing market look like before a sale with tax owed?
sections.html:
Federal numbers on the QuickFacts page for Lucas County show 423,347 people as of July 2025 and 201,974 housing units. Between 2020 and 2024 the typical owned home was worth $163,900 and the typical household took in $62,224. Owners hold 62.0 percent of homes, and monthly gross rent was $934 at the median.

Deeds also pass through the Auditor before recording. The Auditor's transfer fact sheet prints $0.50 per parcel plus $4.00 for each $1,000 of price. Death, survivorship and own-trust transfers are generally exempt from the larger charge. Unpaid tax stays attached to the parcel, so get the Treasurer's balance for yours before signing a contract.

faqs.q: By what date must I contest a Lucas County value?
faqs.a: March 31. The Board of Revision accepts complaints from January 1 through March 31, and the Auditor says that window is set by Ohio law. State law allows the later date of March 31 or the close of first-half collection for the tax year.

faqs.q: Can the Lucas County Board of Revision lower my tax rate?
faqs.a: No. The Auditor states that the board hears appeals on property values only, not on the taxes themselves. Levy rates come from votes in your taxing district.

faqs.q: How do I prove a Lucas County value is wrong?
faqs.a: Bring evidence such as comparable neighborhood sales, a recent sale of the property or a private appraisal. The Auditor's guide says the burden of proof sits with the owner who files.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for the Lucas County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Homeowners aged 65 or more, or totally and permanently disabled, who live in the house and had $41,000 or less in 2025 taxable income. Veterans rated 100 percent disabled and surviving spouses of first responders killed on duty also qualify, with a larger exempted amount.

faqs.q: Is a postmarked check still safe for a Lucas County tax payment?
faqs.a: Not always. The Treasurer warns that USPS postmarks can show a later date than the day you mail, and Ohio law uses the postmark date. Pay online or request a hand-stamped postmark.
